text: The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications is a community-maintained risk catalog from the Open Worldwide Application Security Project — the same organization behind the web application Top 10, a baseline reference in appsec for two decades. It gives security engineers a common vocabulary for risks that show up repeatedly in real LLM systems, the same way the classic list already does for web apps.

Start at the input and data layer. Prompt Injection is attacker-crafted input making the model ignore its instructions, delivered directly by a user or indirectly through a document the model processes. Insecure Output Handling is the mirror image on the way out — treating LLM output as safe and passing it into a database query or rendered HTML without the validation you'd apply to any other untrusted input. Training Data Poisoning corrupts what the model learns, so attacker-chosen behavior only surfaces later, under specific conditions.

At the system and supply chain layer: Model Denial of Service is input crafted to burn disproportionate compute or context-window resources. Supply Chain Vulnerabilities is risk inherited from third-party models, datasets, or plugins — the same problem as a vulnerable open-source package, applied to the AI supply chain. Sensitive Information Disclosure covers an LLM revealing data it memorized, data leaked from a connected tool, or secrets left carelessly in a system prompt.

At the action and trust layer: Insecure Plugin Design is a tool an LLM can call with no validation of its own. Excessive Agency is granting an agent more permissions than its task requires, so a manipulated model can cascade into a real action. Overreliance is trusting LLM output as authoritative without verification. And Model Theft is unauthorized copying of a proprietary model's weights — theft of the product itself.

Here's the pattern worth remembering over memorizing ten isolated names: most trace back to one root cause — no reliable boundary between trusted instructions and untrusted content on the input side, and none between probabilistic output and something a system should trust automatically on the output side. Prompt Injection and Insecure Output Handling are that same gap seen from two directions. Excessive Agency and Insecure Plugin Design are what happens when that gap gets wired directly into real actions.

This list sits alongside the classic OWASP Top 10, not instead of it — an LLM feature is still a web app underneath, needing the same authentication and data fundamentals. Next: the framework that structures how an organization governs and manages this risk end to end, NIST's AI Risk Management Framework.
